recipe: Every program's purpose is transforming data. If you don't understand the data, you don't understand the problem. Understand the data first, the transformation second, the code last.
source_name: Mike Acton, "Data-Oriented Design and C++", CppCon 2014
trigger_condition: Designing or restructuring code whose main job is processing a significant amount of data.

recipe: Three lies: software is a platform, code should model the world, code matters more than data. Hardware is the platform. Data is the problem. Code is only the transformation.
source_name: Mike Acton, "Data-Oriented Design and C++", CppCon 2014
trigger_condition: Is the task primarily data transformation?

recipe: Where there is one, there are many. Design the array first, the single item second. Look along the time axis too: one thing across many frames is also many.
source_name: Richard Fabian, "Data-Oriented Design" (dodbook)
trigger_condition: Are there multiple instances of the same item?

recipe: Solve for the actual data in the common case, not the general case. Generic solutions to imagined future data cost real performance now. Future-proofing is speculation, not engineering.
source_name: Mike Acton, "Data-Oriented Design and C++", CppCon 2014
trigger_condition: Choosing between a general-purpose solution and one tailored to the data the code actually sees.
_review_reason: trigger was missing or not a usable condition

recipe: If you don't understand the cost of the data, you don't understand the cost of the problem. A main-memory miss costs hundreds of cycles; arithmetic is nearly free beside it.
source_name: Data-oriented design (Wikipedia), summarizing Acton/Fabian
trigger_condition: Does the code access large data from main memory?

recipe: The compiler can't fix memory layout: it doesn't know your data's access patterns. Choose the layout yourself instead of expecting optimization flags to recover cache performance.
source_name: Mike Acton, "Data-Oriented Design and C++", CppCon 2014
trigger_condition: Does the performance problem involve memory layout?
_original_recipe: The compiler is not magic. It fixes roughly a tenth of your performance problem and cannot fix memory layout. It doesn't know your data; you do.
_review_reason: 'fixes roughly a tenth' is an unsourced figure; keep the actionable point

recipe: When hot loops touch only some fields of each record, prefer structure-of-arrays: split by access pattern so each pass pulls only the cache lines it uses. Keep array-of-structures when fields are always used together.
source_name: Data-oriented design (Wikipedia); AoS vs SoA / parallel arrays
trigger_condition: Does the hot loop access only one field per record?
_original_recipe: Prefer structure-of-arrays. Split a record by access pattern so a pass over one field touches only cache lines it will actually use. Array-of-structures drags cold bytes through cache.
_review_reason: overstated: SoA wins only when passes touch a subset of fields

recipe: Hot/cold split: fields touched every tick live in one array; rarely-read fields live elsewhere, reached by index. Cold data inside a hot loop is pure wasted bandwidth.
source_name: Richard Fabian, "Data-Oriented Design" (dodbook)
trigger_condition: Does the hot loop read rarely-read fields?

recipe: Avoid pointer chasing. Replace pointers with indices into arrays: smaller, relocatable, serializable, prefetchable. A linked structure is one cache miss per node with no prefetch.
source_name: Richard Fabian, "Data-Oriented Design" (dodbook)
trigger_condition: Does the code traverse linked nodes by following pointers?

recipe: Shrink your handles. u32 or even u16 indices are usually enough and cost a quarter to half of a 64-bit pointer. Smaller elements mean more of them per cache line.
source_name: Andrew Kelley, "Practical Data Oriented Design", Handmade Seattle 2021
trigger_condition: Choosing the type for handles or indices into arrays of entities or nodes.
_review_reason: trigger was missing or not a usable condition

recipe: In C/C++ or Rust `#[repr(C)]` structs, order fields by descending alignment to remove padding and count the wasted bytes (default Rust repr already reorders). Fitting a hot struct in fewer cache lines changes the whole loop's cost.
source_name: Andrew Kelley, "Practical Data Oriented Design", Handmade Seattle 2021
_original_recipe: Order struct fields by descending alignment to kill padding. Count the wasted bytes explicitly. A struct that drops under a cache line changes the behaviour of the entire loop.
trigger_condition: Defining a struct stored in large arrays or passed across an FFI boundary.
_review_reason: Rust's default repr already reorders fields; scope to C/C++/repr(C); trigger was None

recipe: In Zig, `std.MultiArrayList(T)` stores one array per field behind a single list API, removing padding; reach for it before hand-splitting a struct into SoA.
source_name: Andrew Kelley, "Practical Data Oriented Design", Handmade Seattle 2021
_original_recipe: Zig's MultiArrayList is the pattern worth stealing: one logical list, one array per field, same API, padding gone. Reach for that before hand-splitting a struct.
trigger_condition: Writing Zig code that stores many structs and iterates over a subset of fields.
_review_reason: Zig-only advice stated as universal; trigger was None

recipe: Transform in bulk. One function over N items beats N virtual calls over one item: amortized branches, warm instruction cache, obvious vectorization, prefetch that actually works.
source_name: Mike Acton, "Data-Oriented Design and C++", CppCon 2014
trigger_condition: The code calls a function or virtual method once per item over a large collection.
_review_reason: trigger was missing or not a usable condition

recipe: Existence-based processing: don't store a flag and branch on it. Store the entity in the table for that state. Presence is the predicate, so the loop has no if.
source_name: Richard Fabian, "Data-Oriented Design", ch. Existence Based Processing
trigger_condition: A loop over many entities branches on a per-entity boolean state flag.
_review_reason: trigger 'branches on a boolean flag' fires on nearly all code

recipe: Branching is a memory-layout problem. Sort or partition so each pass is homogeneous; the branch then disappears instead of being mispredicted a million times per frame.
source_name: Richard Fabian, "Data-Oriented Design"
trigger_condition: Does the loop branch on a per-item field?

recipe: Condition tables over nested ifs: express decisions as rows of conditions and consequences, then evaluate them as data. Branch-light, inspectable, hot-reloadable, extendable without touching code.
source_name: Richard Fabian, "Data-Oriented Design", ch. Condition Tables
trigger_condition: Game or rule logic is expressed as deeply nested if/else over several conditions.
_review_reason: trigger 'uses nested if statements' fires on nearly all code

recipe: Your data is already a database; you just hid it inside objects. Normalize: entities get ids, relationships get tables. Schema-first exposes multiplicity and frees layout from the class.
source_name: Richard Fabian, "Data-Oriented Design", ch. Relational Databases
trigger_condition: Are objects storing relational data?

recipe: Any data structure is a trade between performance, readability, maintenance, extensibility and reuse. Name which one you are buying before you defend the layout you picked.

recipe: Entity is a bare id. Component is plain data with no behaviour. System is a function over everything holding a given component set. Behaviour binds to data shape, not class.
source_name: Sander Mertens, ECS FAQ
trigger_condition: Designing or implementing an entity-component-system.
_review_reason: trigger was missing or not a usable condition

recipe: Archetype storage groups entities by exact component set: contiguous, fast to query and iterate, but add/remove moves a row between tables. Sparse sets invert it: cheap add/remove, slower joins.
source_name: Sander Mertens, ECS FAQ
trigger_condition: Do entities change their component set at runtime?

recipe: In Bevy, choose storage per component: default Table storage for components iterated every frame, `#[component(storage = "SparseSet")]` for tag-like components added and removed often.
source_name: bevy_ecs documentation (Table vs SparseSet storage)
trigger_condition: Does the code use Bevy components with different iteration patterns?
_original_recipe: Choose storage per component, not per engine. Table storage for components iterated every tick; sparse-set for tag-like components toggled constantly. Bevy makes exactly this a per-component decision.
_review_reason: add the concrete Bevy attribute

recipe: In EnTT, a view iterates the smallest pool and probes the others; an owning group rearranges pools so one hot query iterates contiguously. Use groups only for queries whose join cost shows in profiles.
source_name: EnTT documentation, views vs groups
trigger_condition: Does a hot query join two data pools?
_original_recipe: Pay for the join only where it hurts. An ad-hoc view iterates the smallest pool and probes the rest; an owning group pre-arranges memory so one hot query iterates directly.
_review_reason: name the library whose view/owning-group terms these are (EnTT)

recipe: Entity ids carry a generation. Recycled ids bump the version, so a stale handle compares unequal instead of silently aliasing a new entity. Dangling-reference detection for a few bits.
source_name: EnTT documentation, entity identifiers and versions
trigger_condition: Do entity ids get reused after deletion?

recipe: Pointer stability is a layout decision, not an accident. Page the backing storage, or tombstone on delete, if references must survive growth. Otherwise use indices and let it reallocate.
source_name: EnTT documentation, paged storage and in-place deletion
trigger_condition: Do references need to survive container growth?

recipe: Write the usage code first, concretely. Extract the shared part only after seeing it twice. Make code usable before you make it reusable; abstractions invented up front fit nothing.
source_name: Casey Muratori, "Semantic Compression"
trigger_condition: Will the same concrete code be needed in two places?

recipe: Measure on real data at real sizes. Toy benchmarks fit in cache and lie. The profile decides the layout; the paradigm never does.
source_name: Mike Acton, "Data-Oriented Design and C++", CppCon 2014

recipe: In OCaml (Jane Street style): snake_case for values, functions, fields and file names; Capitalized module and constructor names. In other languages follow their own convention (camelCase in TypeScript).
source_name: Jane Street Base/Core source conventions
_original_recipe: snake_case for values, functions, fields and file names; Capitalized for modules and constructors. Never camelCase. The casing alone tells you what kind of thing you're looking at.
trigger_condition: Writing or naming OCaml code.
_review_reason: 'Never camelCase' is OCaml/Jane Street style and harmful for TypeScript work; scope it

recipe: In OCaml, give each main type its own module and name it `t` (`Order.t`, not `order_t`); the module is the namespace.
source_name: Jane Street Tech Blog, "Core Principles: uniformity of interface"
trigger_condition: Defining an OCaml type whose name repeats its module name.
_original_recipe: One type, one module, and name the type t. Order.t, not order_t. The module is the namespace, so the type name carries no redundant prefix.
_review_reason: OCaml-specific; scope it

recipe: In OCaml (Jane Street Base style) the primary `t` comes first: `Map.find t key`, `Queue.enqueue t x`. Uniform argument order beats locally optimal partial application.
source_name: Jane Street Tech Blog, "Core Principles: uniformity of interface"
_original_recipe: The primary t comes first: Map.find t key, Queue.enqueue t x. Uniform argument order beats locally optimal partial application; predictability is worth more than one clever pipeline.
trigger_condition: Designing function signatures for an OCaml module's main type.
_review_reason: OCaml-specific; trigger was None

recipe: In OCaml, name conversions `of_`/`to_` after the other type and keep them in pairs (`Int.of_string`, `Int.to_string`). Other languages have their own idioms (Rust `From`/`Into`).
source_name: Jane Street Tech Blog, "Core Principles: uniformity of interface"
_original_recipe: Conversions are of_ and to_, named for the other type and kept in pairs: Int.of_string, Int.to_string. Not parse, from, as_, convert, or make.
trigger_condition: Naming conversion functions in OCaml.
_review_reason: OCaml convention stated as universal ('not from, as_' contradicts Rust idioms); trigger was None

recipe: In Jane Street Base, the unsuffixed name is total and returns an option (`Map.find`); the raising twin carries `_exn` (`Map.find_exn`), so partiality is visible at the call site.
source_name: Jane Street Tech Blog, "Core Principles: uniformity of interface"
_original_recipe: The unsuffixed name is total and returns an option; _exn marks the raising twin. Map.find versus Map.find_exn. The suffix is the warning, visible at the call site.
trigger_condition: Naming an OCaml function that may fail to find or produce a value.
_review_reason: Base-specific; trigger was None

recipe: When the plain name already raises (OCaml `of_string`), add an `_opt` variant returning an option (`of_string_opt`) instead of a sentinel like -1 or null.
source_name: Jane Street Base, int_intf.ml (of_string / of_string_opt / *_exn)
_original_recipe: Use _opt when the plain name is already taken by the raising one: of_string raises, of_string_opt returns None. Never a sentinel, never -1, never null.
trigger_condition: A parsing or lookup function needs a non-raising variant.

recipe: Spell it out: configuration not cfg, index not idx, request not req. An abbreviation saves keystrokes once and costs comprehension forever. Allow only ones that read as words.
source_name: Jane Street Base/Core naming practice (observed in source)
trigger_condition: Does the code use abbreviations that are not words?

recipe: Name functions verb-first (create, find, fold, iter, to_list); keep nouns for values and types.
source_name: Jane Street Base, list.mli (observed naming)
trigger_condition: Are function names nouns instead of verbs?
_original_recipe: Functions read verb-first: create, find, fold, iter, to_list. Nouns are values and types. A function named like a noun is usually an accessor you should have exposed instead.

recipe: Make illegal states unrepresentable. Three optional fields is eight states when you meant three. Use a variant whose every case carries exactly the data that case actually has.

recipe: Kill boolean parameters. f ~force:true says nothing at the call site. A two-constructor variant names both sides and survives the third case you will inevitably add.

recipe: Match exhaustively; no catch-all wildcard on your own variants. The underscore turns every future constructor from a compile error into a silent wrong answer.

recipe: In OCaml: return `option` for one obvious failure mode, a variant when callers must branch on the reason, and `Or_error.t` when the error only needs to propagate with context.
source_name: Jane Street Tech Blog, "How to fail -- introducing Or_error.t"
trigger_condition: Does the codebase need callers to branch on failure reason?
_original_recipe: Option for one obvious failure mode, a variant when callers must branch on why, Or_error.t when the error just needs to propagate with context. Pick one per codebase.
_review_reason: 'Pick one per codebase' contradicts the first sentence; Or_error.t is OCaml-specific

recipe: Raise only in exceptional cases; expected absence is a value. Jane Street Base's `List.find` returns an option (Stdlib's raises `Not_found`; use `List.find_opt` there).
source_name: Jane Street Tech Blog, "Core Principles: uniformity of interface"
trigger_condition: Does the code expect missing values as normal results?
_original_recipe: Raise only in genuinely exceptional circumstances. Expected absence is a value, not an exception: List.find returns an option rather than throwing Not_found.
_review_reason: Stdlib List.find raises Not_found; only Base's returns an option

recipe: Label arguments whose type doesn't identify them (OCaml `~f`, `~init`, `~pos`, `~len`; an options object in TypeScript). Two adjacent unlabelled ints are an argument swap waiting to happen.
source_name: Jane Street Base, list.mli (~f, ~init labelled arguments)
trigger_condition: A function takes two or more adjacent arguments of the same primitive type.
_original_recipe: Label any argument whose type doesn't identify it: ~f, ~init, ~pos, ~len. Two adjacent unlabelled ints are an argument swap waiting to happen.

recipe: In Jane Street Core, implement the standard signatures (Comparable, Hashable, Stringable, Sexpable) rather than ad-hoc equivalents, so containers and functors compose without adapters.
source_name: Jane Street Tech Blog, "Core Principles: uniformity of interface"
trigger_condition: Defining an OCaml type that needs comparison, hashing, string or sexp conversion.
_original_recipe: Reuse signatures instead of reinventing them. Comparable, Hashable, Stringable, Sexpable mean the same names and types everywhere, so containers and functors compose without adapter layers.

recipe: Consistency outranks local taste. A convention followed everywhere beats a better convention followed in half the modules, because it makes the API guessable without reading it.
